articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO; Trump says he 'convinced' board
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO; Trump says he 'convinced' board
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock rose more than 30% Monday after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company.
"The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said.
"We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia's CFO."
Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
Patrick Moorhead joins Yahoo Finance executive editor Brian Sozzi to discuss Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia.
President Trump personally intervened to help convince the Nvidia ( NVDA ) board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday.
According to The New York Times , Trump tasked Vice President J.D. Vance with speaking with Huang and the Nvidia board provide assurances that Huang wasn't a national security risk and that he wasn't facing any charges related to alleged chip smuggling to China.
Trump and Huang have developed a close relationship with Huang frequently praising the president's stances on various tech policy issues and Trump lauding Huang's business acumen.
Huang previously resigned from Nvidia following revelations about multiple affairs including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and two reported relationship with Nvidia employees.
During the company's Q3 earning call last week, board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intent to bring Huang back as CEO.
EMJ Capital founder and president Eric Jackson joins Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi to discuss Nvidia ( NVDA ) reinstating Jensen Huang as its CEO and how his ousting will leave him more focused and more careful.
As Nvidia's stock is gaining almost $1 trillion on the announcement of co-founder Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO, former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein shared a change of heart on the matter.
The Wall Street veteran revisited an observation he had made following Huang's ouster earlier this month, where he referenced [Charles] de Gaulle's quote, "The graveyards are filled with indispensable men."
"Guess you can come back from the graveyard if you're really, really, really indispensable," Blankfein wrote Monday . "The NVDA board will not have that opportunity," he added.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) surged on Monday following Jensen Huang's surprise reinstatement as CEO, sparking a massive rally across US stocks. Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott warns of reading too much into the massive bounce.
Much of the move is being supercharged by Wall Street with "a massive surge of MECHANICAL buying," short sellers getting forced out of their downside bets, and options dealers scrambling to unwind hedges.
"AI and Equities are 'Too Big To Fail," wrote McElligott. Still, the strategist warns investors not to mistake a forced short-covering rally for an all-clear signal on the economy.
"It's naïve to believe that a one-day 'Up Shock' absolves the market of underlying concerns surrounding the multiple spinning plates," he wrote. "This 'Mechanical Bounce' guarantees us nothing."
McElligott added that a single-day surge does not erase broader structural headwinds—including stubborn inflation, rising borrowing costs, and cooling expectations around corporate AI spending. If those pressures persist, he noted, investors could abandon their decade-long playbook of buying every stock market dip and begin shifting money into cash and bonds instead.
Twelve days without Jensen Huang cost Nvidia ( NVDA ) about $1.2 trillion. His first day back is winning most of it back in a way Wall Street hasn't seen since Cisco ( CSCO ) in 2001.
The chipmaker's board reinstated Huang as CEO Monday, and President Trump says he " convinced " them. "I don't think anybody could revive the stock like it's being revived right now," Trump said.
The stock is up about 30%, putting Nvidia on track to add more than $900 billion in market value. That would be the biggest one-day gain ever. The old record, Microsoft's ( MSFT ) $450 billion jump in July, isn't even half of it. It also tops the record one-day loss, Nvidia's own $593 billion drop on DeepSeek day in January 2025. Read more .
While Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock price might be soaring thanks to the return of Jensen Huang as CEO, the board's decision to bring him back has still leaves unanswered questions at the company, William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji wrote in an investor note Monday.
"The events of recent weeks have exposed deeper questions around corporate governance, leadership succession, and regulatory oversight that could have lasting implications for the company's competitive position, Naji said.
In a statement ahead of the start of trading on Wall Street Monday, Nvidia's said it's board "received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."
President Trump on Monday praised the board's decision, noting that he pushed for Huang's reinstatement.
Reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees, I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around."
Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor Brian Sozzi and anchor Julie Hyman discuss what might happen if longtime Nvidia CFO Colette Kress leaves the company.
Nvidia staff welcome back Jensen Huang as CEO, according to an employee's X post.
Most of the people pictured in the video cheer Huang's return. However, one engineer who spoke to YF on condition of anonymity said, "This is the worst outcome. We already paid the price of his departure but are still saddled with working for a jerk."
While some on Wall Street see the Nvidia board's decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO as a benefit, others like KeyBanc Capital Markets' John Vinh are skeptical that it's a pure positive for the company.
In a note Monday, Vinh wrote that he remained sector weight on Nvidia's stock noting that "there's still uncertainty regarding the potential for [additional] developments that may be uncovered as part of the board's investigation, as well as the SEC investigation into accounting issues."
UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri wrote in a note on Monday that the Nvidia ( NVDA ) board's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO was a clear positive for the company.
The board made the announcement ahead of the start of the trading day, sending Nvidia stock soaring.
In his note, Arcuri says Huang's return should also quite concerns about financing, talent retention, and Nvidia's supply chain strategy.
Still, he says that Nvidia could soon be forced to adjust its management structure and develop a succession plan.
More broadly, Arcuri says the entire Nvidia episode could lead to more hawkish export controls.
Michael Burry, the legendary short seller who rose to prominence after predicting the great financial crisis, responded to the news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement on Monday, calling the company "weaker, more craven than even I thought."
In his post on X, Burry urged the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission to continue their investigations into Nvidia.
Burry revealed a bearish position on Nvidia in November of last year and has been a longstanding critic of the company. On Friday, Burry posted an update on his Substack, sharing that he sold half of his put options on Nvidia and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

articles.title_orig: Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan at meeting in China, urged U.S. to halt arms sale
articles.title_zh: Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan at meeting in China, urged U.S. to halt arms sale
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."
Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.
Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."
Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.
Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.
Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.
Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.
Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

Charles Gasparino is out with an interesting report. He argues that the Nvidia saga isn't over and for reasons that could rattle the equity bulls.
The drama is no surprise but this is a concern:
Now it's not clear that "stuff that is coming out" means news we already know about or conjecture but it's a reminder that there are powerful forces that don't like how Nvidia has behaved and don't want to see Huang succeed. Now maybe it's China hawks in a power play and they've now had their wings clipped or maybe the people fighting against open source AI really want to take Huang down.
So now we just have to wait for the next round of leaks. No one likes to hear about accounting leaks and the vendor finance is a real problem.
Shares are up 30% today but they've flatlined from the open. When people hear about accounting issues, they're inclined to take some off the table.

articles.title_orig: House Foreign Affairs Committtee still expects Nvidia CEO to testify Dec. 1
articles.title_zh: House Foreign Affairs Committtee still expects Nvidia CEO to testify Dec. 1
articles.content_orig:
NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., about congressional efforts to question Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about China's access to Nvidia chips.
For more, we're joined now by Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove. She represents California's 37th Congressional District in LA and serves on the House Foreign Relations Committee. She's the top Democrat on the subcommittee on South and Central Asia with jurisdiction over export control, and she and a few of her colleagues say they want some answers from U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Good morning, Congresswoman. Thank you for joining us.
SYDNEY KAMLAGER-DOVE: Good morning. Thanks for having me.
FADEL: Now, you and two of your Democratic colleagues, Jamie Raskin and Gregory Meeks, are asking for more information to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick blocked efforts to restrict Chinese access to Nvidia chips. Lay out your concerns here and what you are looking for.
KAMLAGER-DOVE: Yeah. So the commerce secretary is responsible for protecting our money and our national security. And we think the American people deserve to know if he is doing that, or if he is putting his family's financial interests ahead of our national security. This smells like corruption, and it actually smells like an acute risk to this country's national security.
So we sent this letter because we have a lot of questions. We want to know was the decision to sell these chips to Megaspeed, was it influenced by Jensen Huang, who's a major Trump ally, who donated $25 million to Trump's ballroom? Was it because the commerce secretary's son's investment firm has hundreds of millions of dollars tied up in Nvidia, and that could be affected by the outcome of all of this case?
And we want to know how deep all of this goes. Where are the other implications? Because Howard Lutnick has been personally involved all of the decision-making around these chips deals, and he has been slow-walking rulemaking that would protect our country's national security and our assets like these chips.
FADEL: And you sent the letter to the head of the family firm that his son now runs, which he exited when he joined the Trump administration. I will note that the firm is saying they've done nothing wrong and will show that. Do you suspect that laws were broken?
KAMLAGER-DOVE: I definitely think that there are a lot of backroom deals that have happened to allow companies like Nvidia to sell these kinds of chips to Megaspeed. You know, at one point, Cantor Fitzgerald actually owned 3.5 million shares of Nvidia. That's a lot. That's worth about $1.3 billion. And once the White House started investigating Megaspeed, A, Howard Lutnick asked all of this investigations - all of these investigations to be shifted to DOJ. And then also, Cantor Fitzgerald started divesting in those shares.
But we also know that these are very important chips. You know, they're really special. They run military. They run our banks, our water infrastructure, things like the NSA. And if these chips are getting into the wrong hands, if they're going to China, that puts our country at risk at the expense of the American people.
FADEL: What do you see as the appropriate limits to put on the export of these semiconductor chips?
KAMLAGER-DOVE: Well, we have been asking all of these questions for over a year, and there has been so little traction with this last Congress. And we've said, If you have some of these bad actors that are on these do-not-sell lists, why are you finding ways to work around those lists so that companies can sell to other companies that can then - and will - sell these chips to China?
It is a problem because once these chips leave our hands, we cannot get them back. And we are giving our adversaries the opportunity to catch up with us and advance our technologies and put the American people in harm's way. We need a much more robust rulemaking system, and we need secretaries that will adhere to those laws rather than finding a way to work around them, either to put Americans at risk or to make money for themselves and Trump's inner circle.
FADEL: Republican Senator Tim Scott, who chairs the Senate banking committee, formally invited Lutnick to appear for a public hearing next month on Nvidia and chip exports. Does that give you confidence in a thorough bipartisan inquiry here?
KAMLAGER-DOVE: I hope so. National security is a bipartisan issue, and we should all be motivated to want to get to the bottom of this and to stop this from happening. This is costing Americans money, and at some point, we could be costing Americans' lives. And I would hope that Republicans and Democrats could stand together and say no more of this.
FADEL: Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove is the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia. Thank you for joining us.
KAMLAGER-DOVE: Thank you so much.

Elon Musk ’s SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp has been accused of profiting off its AI model Grok that produces child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual sexual images from photographs while failing to put safeguards in place to stop it.
Virginia and Oregon sued the company after several state attorneys general had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months.
The choices that went into building Grok led to a proliferation of child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual intimate imagery on the companies' platforms, the lawsuit alleges.
The companies prioritized their business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity," Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”
Oregon also filed a lawsuit Monday. The attorneys general brought their separate but similar cases under their states' consumer protection statutes.
The lawsuits named as defendants several Musk companies and subsidiaries, including SpaceX, the social platform X, and SpaceX Super Intelligence, or SpaceXSI, the AI subsidiary of SpaceX.
In a statement, SpaceXSI said sexual content involving minors “whether real or AI-generated, is abhorrent. It has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent.”
The company said it had acted promptly to tighten protections when “bad actors” found ways to misuse Grok's image- and video-generation tool. If users try to break its safeguards to generate nonconsensual content, the company said, it takes “appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement.”
“Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors,” the statement said.
The lawsuits come at a time of growing concern about AI’s risks for children, from its impact on brain development to the unhealthy relationships many young people have formed with chatbots.
Grok, which can be accessed through Musk's social media platform X, rolled out image generation and editing features to all users in December 2025, according to the Virginia lawsuit. By January, the tool had sparked a global backlash after it became clear Grok users could create realistic-looking but fake sexualized images of people. Researchers warned that some appeared to depict children.
As the Virginia lawsuit put it, “X was flooded with sexualized content — primarily of women.”
At least two countries, Malaysia and Indonesia, announced temporary bans and other nations said they were launching or widening investigations. In response, Grok prevented non-paying users from generating or editing images.
The change didn't stop users from making more non-consensual sexualized images; “it simply made that generation profitable," Virginia’s lawsuit said.
The developer of Grok, which was then known as xAI, has since rebranded as SpaceX Super Intelligence.
Virginia argued that most major AI developers designed their products so they could not be used to produce sexualized images to avoid the generation of nonconsensual content.
“Defendants declined to implement these safeguards. Defendants’ published system prompt materials — the set of instructions that guides the AI model’s behavior — told Grok to ‘assume good intent,’ stated that terms such as ‘teenage’ or ‘girl’ do not necessarily imply underage, and imposed minimal restrictions on sexual content," the lawsuit said.
The lawsuit noted that xAI marketed Grok from the outset as a tool that would “answer spicy questions that are rejected by most other AI systems.”
And it argued X made “false, deceptive or misleading” statements in January about changes intended to prevent Grok from allowing users to edit images of real people in revealing clothes.
Users could still create nonconsensual sexualized imagery through a standalone app and website, the lawsuit said. And when users openly traded “jailbreak” prompts to get around what limits Grok did have on sexualized images, Musk’s companies failed to promptly address the exploits, the Virginia lawsuit alleged.
Both lawsuits draw heavily on news outlets’ investigative reporting about the rollout of the tool, the backlash and the company’s response to it.
Virginia's lawsuit, filed in a state court in Richmond, argued that the Musk companies violated the state's consumer protection law by "misrepresenting that they implemented and enforced safeguards to protect consumers from exposure" to harmful sexualized imagery on their platforms.
It asked the court for $2,500 for each “willful violation” of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, with an exact number to be proven at trial.
It also asked a judge to prevent the companies from further violating the consumer protection laws and force the defendants to give up any “ill-gotten gains” acquired in connection with the alleged violations.
The Oregon lawsuit makes a similar request.
“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable," Jones said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board shows "lack of backbone" in re-hiring Jensen Huang, governance experts say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s intense boardroom drama, in which Jensen Huang was ousted and brought back in the span of less than two weeks, would not have been possible without questionable decisions by Nvidia’s directors.
Now, the board faces intense scrutiny over its role in a corporate soap opera with enormous consequences.
While Wall Street loves the shocking return of Huang at the helm of Nvidia, corporate governance experts are horrified by what they view as malpractice by the company’s board: With no chair prior to Huang’s ouster, no succession plan and the loosest of leashes on its CEO, the board had set itself up to fail.
Huang said he built the company so that he alone could run it – and the stock acted that way, losing $1.5 trillion in market value since the scandal erupted on Nov. 8. An outpouring of support for Huang from investors and partners followed, and a shareholder revolt seemed imminent.
The board, consisting of many long-tenured Huang supporters, announced its decision to reinstate Huang on Monday, after the same board unanimously accepted his resignation. And directors are bringing Huang back before the completion of a board-ordered investigation that was supposed to get to the bottom of allegations over whether Huang has been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
President Donald Trump on Monday told CNBC he called the board and helped orchestrate Huang’s return. That put the board in a no-win scenario: Stand pat and risk getting ousted. Give in and appear weak and ineffective. (Nvidia declined to comment.)
Of course, it didn’t have to be this way. A strong board – one that provides vigorous oversight of the CEO and requires successors to be groomed – could have avoided this mess turning into a debacle.
“The board should resign. Every one of them,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. “This is a complete failure of corporate governance.”
Huang stands accused of some serious violations of corporate policy. He acknowledged an affair after reports of a relationship with a major customer, and he was reportedly in a relationship with an employee.
Although the board on Monday said US government officials assured them rehiring Huang posed no national security risk, the investigation continues.
The seriousness of the allegations make Huang’s return all the more shocking from a corporate governance standpoint.
“The standard to apply is: Would we fire a middle manager for this behavior?” said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors. Potential espionage aside, Huang’s affairs would be grounds for dismissal, Minow argued.
Minow said she would favor the board resigning except that she fears Huang would just bring in people who are “even more compliant.”
But the board appears to have been backed into a corner.
The Nvidia scandal contributed to a market meltdown so severe that some suggested the AI bubble was popping before our eyes.
Huang was the He-Man CEO of AI, the industry’s de facto central banker and widely viewed as a visionary pioneer who transformed graphics processors into the lifeblood of AI computing. And he is buddies with the president of the United States.
Trump on Monday was effusive with praise for Huang, telling CNBC he personally called Huang and the board to help arrange his comeback.
“With pressure from the president and his administration, the board may have felt it had no choice, but this is not a board that has ever shown that it understands its obligations to shareholders or to the law,” Minow said.
The board failed by placing Huang above corporate governance, said Bill George, former CEO of Medtronic.
“The board does not appear to be in control,” said George, now an executive fellow at Harvard Business School.
The board didn’t have to let it get to this point.
For example, it could have opted to put Huang on leave pending the results of the investigation, which could have insulated it from outside pressure – even from the commander in chief.
But the problems started earlier. Without a succession plan, Huang effectively held the board hostage, said Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor.
Most well-run companies with functional boards have an emergency plan in place, in case the CEO is hit by a bus, suddenly resigns or needs to be disciplined. They also typically review potential replacement CEO candidates as part of their due diligence. There’s no evidence Nvidia had done any of that.
That, in part, gave Huang an aura of invincibility .
“Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” Huang told Bloomberg in 2023. “So, for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.”
Nvidia has a deeply talented bench. So allowing a company to rely on a singular figure – who alone could account for trillions of dollars of company value – represents a complete failure of the board, Sonnenfeld argued.
Still, the board’s flip-flop may not be nefarious.
Ultimately, the board is tasked with deciding whether it can trust Huang and whether his ongoing presence at Nvidia is in the best interest of the company and its stockholders, noted Brittany Rogers, partner in the corporate governance practice at O’Melveny & Myers.
“There is no single ‘right’ answer here,” she said, calling the decision complex and difficult.
Although it may be easy to assign bad motives to the decision to rehire Huang, the board may also have been presented with new facts that changed its mind – even from a week earlier.
“I would apply the presumptions of the business judgment rule and assume that the directors acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief that each decision served Nvidia’s best interests,” said Lawrence Cunningham, director of the University of Delaware’s Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance.

Save $70 right now.

The iPad (11th Gen) remains the best Apple tablet for most people. In our iPad 11 review , we said it has significantly improved performance thanks to its A16 chip, longer battery life, and a larger 128GB starting storage option; Save $50 right now.
It's not the newest model, but the llast-gen iPad mini 7 is still a great compact tablet that's now on sale for Black Friday with $150 off. In our iPad mini 7 review , we said delivers excellent performance and battery life while retaining its predecessor's vibrant display and portable design.
It's a minor discount, but we'll take it. The MacBook Neo sports a 13-inch Liquid Retina (2408 x 1506) display, A18 Pro chipset, 8GB of RAM, 256GB SSD, and 1080p FaceTime HD camera. In our MacBook Neo review , we said no other laptop comes close in terms of bang for your buck.
The 13-inch MacBook Air M4 features the same elegant design as its predecessors, along with excellent M4-driven performance and epic battery life. This starting configuration comes with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD. Right now you can get $250 off, which is a great discount.

Right now, you can pick up the Eero Pro 7 in a three-pack for $599 at Amazon . Alternatively, if you live somewhere smaller, you can get a two-pack for just $399 . In our Eero Pro 7 review , we loved how compact these new mesh devices are and the fact that they ship with two, high-speed 5 Gigabit Ethernet ports around back.
If you're looking for one of the best all-in-one computers, you can't go wrong with Apple's iMac. Right now, you can get the new iMac M6 for $86 off at Amazon . However, if you want to save even more, the iMac M4 is down to $1,199 or $300 off its normal price.

Though I haven't tried the iMac M4, in my iMac M6 review I praised its speedy performance and the fact that it now ships with Apple's proprietary N1 networking chip which adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 support.
If you’ve been using a Mac for some time, then you’ve likely heard of Satechi. For those who haven’t though, the company makes Apple accessories that look and feel like they were made by Cupertino itself. I’ve used their Hub & Stand with my Mac mini as well as their mechanical keyboards and both haven't let me down yet. articles.title_orig: Oregon-raised Nvidia CEO reinstated after China spy scandal
articles.title_zh: Oregon-raised Nvidia CEO reinstated after China spy scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Eleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds.
On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)
But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”
The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession.
But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return.
Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.
The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.
But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.
And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.
Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.
The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis.
It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.
But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.
The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology.
But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.
With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.
The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times , alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse.
Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee.
But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks."
As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.
That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions.
“Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday.
Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.
Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani to Cap E-Bike Rides at $3.65 for Citi Bike Members Starting Next Year
articles.title_zh: Mamdani to Cap E-Bike Rides at $3.65 for Citi Bike Members Starting Next Year
articles.content_orig:
Lyft will cap the Citi Bike member cost of any sub-45-minute e-bike trip at $3.65 starting on Jan. 19, Mayor Mamdani said on Monday, and the bike-share provider has also agreed to freeze member rates through the middle of 2029.
The Citi Bike-loving mayor’s announcement — first reported in the New York Times —comes ahead of a City Council hearing on Citi Bike fees scheduled for Dec. 2. All four bills on the meeting’s agenda would offer discount rides or cap rider fees. Council Speaker Julie Menin is scheduled to appear at the mayor’s Citi Bike announcement on Monday morning.
Lyft made $24 million off the bike-share system last year, according to publicly posted Citi Bike financial reports. Annual membership, meanwhile, has skyrocketed from $95 in 2013 to $239 today. Citi Bike’s only existing e-bike ride price cap is $5.40 for sub-45-minute trips into or out of Manhattan; a 45-minute e-bike ride not going into or out of Manhattan currently costs $12.15. Transportation Alternatives’ “Citi Bike Riders Union” campaign has called on the city to cap all e-bike rides at $3.
The company’s contract to run the city’s bike-share program expires on May 26, 2029, though no competitor could likely come close to meeting the capacity demands of the current Citi Bike system. That gives Lyft significant leverage in negotiations with the city.
Editor’s note: This story initially misreported that the new price cap will apply to e-bike trips into our out of Manhattan; it will apply to all e-bike trips.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian naval drones strike a new Russian warship in Libya, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian naval drones strike a new Russian warship in Libya, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders are becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s China-made adult bed rails recalled after 89-year-old woman dies of suffocation
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s China-made adult bed rails recalled after 89-year-old woman dies of suffocation
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of adult bed rails from China that were sold in the US have been recalled after an 89-year-old woman died of suffocation when she was trapped between the product and her mattress.
About 2,114 adult bed rails sold on Amazon by Guangzhou Yupin Technology Co. – a Chinese company doing business as Xentrawave – are included in the recall, according to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission.
All batches of Xentrawave’s model XT016 and batch number 20251212 of model XT026 are included in the recall for failing to meet mandatory safety requirements, because customers can be pinned between the rail and the side of the mattress – posing a risk of death by asphyxiation.
The XT106 model adult bed rail also doesn’t meet structural stability requirements and its push pins and push pin holes are incorrectly sized, posing a risk of laceration, the agency said.
The CPSC said it has received one report of a death related to the Xentrawave recall, involving the 89-year-old woman who died from asphyxiation.
Customers can find the model numbers XT016 or XT026 on the front of the product’s outer packaging and the first page of the instruction manual.
For the XT026 model, consumers can locate the batch number on the product label attached to the back of the bed rail’s gray fabric pouch and in the instruction manual.
Consumers should immediately stop use of the recalled bed rails and contact Xentrawave for a full refund.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
They will be asked to cut the foam padding on the bed rail handles, disassemble the product and email a photo of the destroyed bed rail to xentrawavedirect@163.com or submit it online at https://xentrawahelp.com/xentrawave-bed-rail-safety-recall/ .
The recalled XT016 bed rails were sold on Amazon from May 2025 through March 2026 and the XT026 model was sold from March 2026 through August 2026. The bed rails cost between $37 and $40.
The bed rails were manufactured by China-based Guangzhou Nanyu Medical Technology Co.

articles.title_orig: Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates
articles.title_zh: Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates
articles.content_orig:
Meduza, Mediazona, and more than a dozen other journalistic teams will present the results of an independent analysis of Russian mortality data tonight, after 5 p.m. CET . The data came from the hacker groups Cyber Partisans of Belarus and SilentCrow, who obtained it after hacking Rosstat’s database.
We and colleagues from other independent outlets spent more than two weeks examining the leak, verifying its authenticity and searching the records Rosstat received from the EGR ZAGS for data on losses among Russian troops since the start of the full-scale war.
All the journalists who worked on this project concluded that the database is largely authentic. Final loss estimates may vary between outlets, depending on how each includes or excludes certain categories of the dead. Not every death can be definitively linked to combat operations, even using the leak’s detailed cause-of-death data. As a result, estimates of Russian military losses vary depending on how that link is interpreted and on the nuances of counting. We will explain in detail why we are confident our own count is accurate.
The EGR ZAGS data in the leak include only registered deaths. For military personnel, the delay between death and registration can run six months or longer, and the share of these late registrations has been growing. As a result, a significant share of the dead are missing even from Rosstat’s internal data, especially over the past year and a half.
Estimating the true number of Russian military losses, accounting for these late registrations, therefore requires research that draws not only on the EGR ZAGS leak but also on many other independently obtained data sets and statistical modeling. Meduza will publish an estimate of these “invisible” deaths alongside its analysis of the Rosstat leak.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected] .
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Leaker Releases All Files for Alleged Xbox Build of Game
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Leaker Releases All Files for Alleged Xbox Build of Game
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The CyberLeek hacking gang claims to have released a key executable program that promises to help the modding community port Grand Theft Auto 6 to the PC.
On Monday, the group updated its website, posting a link to the 57MB archive that contains the executable program. “The exe is out. Always free. An early Christmas gift from CL,” CyberLeek wrote in a post titled “Xmas came early.”
The archive supposedly completes the stolen Xbox build for GTA 6 that CyberLeek initially began circulating last week via a 209GB torrent containing files for Rockstar’s RAGE game engine and the Xbox console. CyberLeek now suggests that the file dump will be enough for the modding community to recompile the game to run on a PC, since the Xbox platform runs on an OS based on Microsoft Windows.
“The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects,” the gang says. CyberLeek also appears to have settled for merely asking for donations to the group’s meme coin after its previous efforts to drive up the coin's market cap flopped .
One community GTA 6 recompilation project, Leonida, has been examining the leaked executable files. Traffic has been so high that the group’s chat server on Discord malfunctioned, appearing to crash. However, an admin later posted: “It will take at least a week for us to get somewhere noticeable to the point where you can play on your pc.” To avoid the project from being taken down, the admin added: “We will not be giving assets whatsoever; you will need to download the game yourself.”
"This .exe file does NOT RUN THE GAME ," an admin also posted before the leak dropped. "This will be used by the developers to work with and make the actual recomp, which will use the game files and exe to build the port."
In the meantime, users in the project have been using AI coding tools and agents, including Anthropic’s Claude, to reverse-engineer and try to get the leaked game files running on Windows. “THE GAME ALMOST BOOTS. BLACK SCREEN, AUDIO CUTS OFF,” claimed one user in the Discord chat.
So far, Rockstar Games and its parent, Take-Two Interactive, haven’t responded to a request for comment. But developers are rumored to be preparing an official PC release for GTA 6 as soon as next year’s first quarter. Still, a pirated PC port could go viral and sap sales for the game, which is currently exclusive to the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.
The dumped files also suggest CyberLeek was able to infiltrate and steal an Xbox copy of GTA 6 well before the game officially launched. Although Take-Two subpoenaed the major platforms, including Microsoft, for records to try to uncover the leaker, CyberLeek remains at large.
I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector.
Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service.
I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard.
I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

NVDA rose 5.8% in overnight trading after dropping 23% in the week, its worst weekly drop since September 2008.
Retail sentiment was 'extremely bullish' for NVDA, 'bullish' for AMD, MU and SNDK, 'bearish' for INTC and SOXX.
AI giant Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq on Thursday after a blockbuster IPO, but the stock lost steam after the opening-day rally.
Tech stocks rebounded sharply in Sunday's overnight trading after a challenging week, as concerns over AI overvaluation appeared to outweigh optimism around Anthropic's (ANT) landmark IPO and another strong quarterly report from Nvidia (NVDA).
Tech analysts such as Dan Ives said that while "bears will feel validation," there is no stopping the AI revolution and that there were "clear areas of safety/winners despite the noise and market backdrop worries."

NVDA stock rose 5.8% in overnight trading after dropping 23% in the week, its worst weekly drop since September 2008. Intel (INTC) gained 4.8%, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) climbed 5.4%. Memory stocks also rallied, with Micron Technology (MU) up 4.6% and SanDisk (SNDK) advancing 5.2%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) rose 4.2%.
"Yelling fire in a crowded theater moment is here and the bears will take center stage with this narrative and ultimately with Jensen out at Nvidia, market fears globally, and the Blue Tidal Wave in DC going after Big Tech this will be bumpy road over the coming months," Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in an X post.
"That said, the technology age of AI is coming one way or another…and this is not going to slow down the 160 GW of backlog/demand power through 2029 vs. ~80 GW-100 GW of capacity build out planned the next few years. This technology wave will continue at high speed and the Blue Wave, bears, China hawks are not stopping this 4th Industrial Revolution."
In a separate post, Ives highlighted Apple (AAPL), cybersecurity players such as CrowdStrike (CRWD) and Palo Alto Networks (PANW), hyperscalers Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL), software firms Palantir (PLTR) and Snowflake (SNOW), and SpaceX (SPCX) as the possible beneficiaries in the tech market.
AI giant Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq on Thursday after a blockbuster IPO. However, after 17% opening day gains, the stock quickly lost steam. Investors pouring billions into the IPO, potentially diverting liquidity from other investments, was cited as one of the reasons behind last week's broader tech selloff.
Meanwhile, they are also closely watching the updates for Nvidia after the ouster of former CEO Jensen Huang and risks from multiple investigations into the AI chipmaker's dealings. Last week, Califonia opened a probe, while Nvidia said it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.
Nvidia's investments and partnerships span dozens of tech companies, making it central to the health of the AI industry. The spy scandal emerged as investors were already questioning the pace of AI spending and the market rally it had fueled.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street analysts cheer Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia — but they still have concerns
articles.title_zh: Wall Street analysts cheer Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia — but they still have concerns
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bernstein analysts were quick to upgrade Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Monday after the board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chipmaker, though Wall Street sees ongoing investigations as a lingering overhang on the company.
The stock surged as much as 32% following Huang's reinstatement. President Trump said he spoke to the board and "convinced" them to reinstate Huang.
Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon and his team, which had downgraded the stock to a Neutral-equivalent Market Perform rating just 11 days ago, rerated the stock as Outperform as soon as the board announced Huang's return.
"As we remain positive on AI buildout fundamentals, and with Jensen back in the seat, we upgrade today back to [Outperform] (as his exit was the primary reason for the downgrade)," Rasgon wrote.
The analyst maintained a $200 price target, highlighting questions that will likely leave some overhang in place, including ongoing investigations which may limit NVDA's multiple for now.
"While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again-off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like," the analysts added, questioning what this says about how the board goes about making other decisions.
Yorkville's Dan Ives, which has maintained a Buy rating on the stock, said on Monday that the firm believes Nvidia stock should be valued at $300 with Jensen Huang back. However, the analysts kept $225 as the price target for the stock, saying they're looking for a resolution of the board's investigation.
The path to closing the price gap "runs through the committee's conclusion, a clean read on the export probe, and a 4Q print delivered by a CEO whose tenure is no longer a topic on the earnings call," Ives wrote.
KeyBank analyst John Vinh stated that while Jensen Huang's reinstatement is a "significantly positive development," the firm retains a Sector Weight, or Neutral, rating and awaits further clarification on the board's ongoing investigation and the SEC accounting inquiry before revisiting its rating,
Stifel analyst Ruben Roy, meanwhile, reiterated a Buy rating and maintained a $205 price target, noting that while Huang's return removes key-person risk, the ongoing investigations remain a potential overhang on the shares.
Several other analysts echoed the sentiment that a major overhang has been cleared, even as governance questions remain. In other words,
"In our view, the reinstatement removes the key overhang created by the CEO transition," Citi analyst Atif Malik wrote, issuing a Buy rating and raising the firm's price target to $240.
Malik noted that while Huang's reinstatement "restores continuity across NVDA's product roadmap," uncertainty remains around the scrutiny into Huang's relationships. "That said, we would view clean resolutions of these concerns as a further catalyst," Malik added.
Others pointed toward Nvidia shares responding to an overcorrection in selling.
Analyst Tristan Gerra noted that while Baird retained its Neutral rating, "near-term the stock has over-corrected and we expect a rerating towards our price target driven by the return of Mr. Huang as CEO."
"I am still a buyer of Nvidia today," Antoine Chkaiban, New Street Research analyst, said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I think there's still plenty of upside with the stock. It's still very cheap. You know we have Nvidia generating 25 bucks of earnings in 2028. So the stock is still trading below ten times that [on a PE ratio]. And I think there's plenty of upside."
Correction: A previous version of this article misstated Stifel's price target. We regret the error.
