articles.title_orig: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
articles.title_zh: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
articles.content_orig:
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event.
Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess.
Previous editions have produced some particularly significant developments. The 2016 show saw the J-20 stealth fighter make its first public flying appearance , while the 2018 edition provided an unusually revealing look at the aircraft, including a demonstration of its internal weapons bays, loaded with air-to-air missiles . The 2022 exhibition featured the J-20 on static display for the first time at Zhuhai, alongside the Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, Z-20 helicopter, and YY-20 aerial refueling tanker, which made its first flying demonstration at the event. More recently, the 2024 exhibition was particularly notable for the public debut of the J-35A stealth fighter and the appearance of the catapult-capable J-15T carrier-based fighter.
This year’s exhibition, scheduled to take place from December 7 to 13, will showcase, among others, a broad range of the PLAN’s capabilities, with a particularly notable emphasis on the rapid evolution of its carrier aviation capabilities, something we have addressed in detail in the past . Among the most noteworthy aircraft expected to feature are the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the operational J-35 stealth fighter, the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, several naval variants of the Z-20 helicopter, and, perhaps most significantly, the new JL-15 carrier-capable trainer, a development of the land-based JL-10 .
While we have seen the J-15T at Zhuhai before, the aircraft will be of particular interest if it is shown with the indigenous WS-10H2 engine. Such a configuration would offer a closer look at the latest evolution of China’s carrier-based Flanker derivative and its ongoing transition toward a more domestically supported carrier aviation ecosystem.
The appearance of the J-35 would be another major highlight. The aircraft represents a significant step in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ambitions, bringing a fifth-generation stealth fighter capability into the carrier air wing. Its presence would provide another opportunity to examine the progress of China’s next-generation naval fighter program. Back in 2014, Zhuhai saw the public debut of the FC-31 fighter demonstrator. At the time, it was still a land-based concept, and export was the main talking point, although there was already speculation about a naval variant, today’s J-35.
Meanwhile, the KJ-600 is arguably one of the most important developments in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ecosystem. The twin-engine turboprop aircraft is designed to provide airborne early warning and battle management capabilities, something that would transform the situational awareness and coordination available to China’s carrier strike groups.
Several variants of the Z-20 family are also expected to feature, reflecting the growing importance of helicopters in carrier operations, including airborne anti-submarine warfare, utility, and other maritime support missions. You can read more about the Z-20 family and other Chinese rotary-wing developments in this previous TWZ deep-dive on the topic .
Perhaps the most intriguing aircraft on the list, however, is the JL-15.
The JL-15 is derived from the Hongdu JL-10, also exported as the L-15 Falcon, a twin-engine advanced jet trainer and lead-in fighter trainer. The navalized development was initially reported to be designated JL-10J, but is now confirmed as being the JL-15. A tailhook-equipped mockup was spotted alongside the aircraft carrier Fujian in 2024. However, its operational status remains unclear, and China is known to have encountered difficulties with its earlier JL-9G naval trainer, whose tailhook was reportedly deleted following structural problems.
Regarding the rumoured JL-10J carrier-capable jet trainer, another hint was spotted next to the carrier Fujian: It appears to be an unfinished JL-10J mockup stored on the dockside . So question is: Two tails as shown in the latest CG or just one like the regular JL-10? pic.twitter.com/BM8W8MRGWK
Its appearance would provide a particularly interesting indication of how China is thinking about training its next generation of carrier-based pilots. A carrier-capable development of the JL-10 would be an important addition to the emerging carrier aviation ecosystem, bridging the gap between conventional jet training and the demanding requirements of operating from an aircraft carrier.
The JL-15 also makes an interesting comparison with the U.S. Navy’s somewhat stuttering efforts to introduce a new training jet for its carrier pilots.
The U.S. Navy’s Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) program is intended to replace its aging fleet of T-45 Goshawk trainers, but the acquisition effort has encountered considerable difficulties. Earlier this month, we described how Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) withdrew its proposed clean-sheet Freedom Jet from the competition, citing concerns over the Navy’s insistence on firm-fixed-price production commitments before the aircraft’s design had sufficiently matured. This leaves the Beechcraft M-346N , based on Leonardo’s established M-346 Master , as the only publicly known remaining contender . The program has also experienced schedule slippage, with the initial contract award now expected in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027.
Perhaps more significant is the difference in the two services’ approaches to carrier aviation training. The U.S. Navy has removed the requirement for its next-generation jet trainer to be capable of operating from an actual aircraft carrier, including carrier qualification and simulated carrier touch-and-goes at land-based facilities. Instead, it increasingly relies on advanced simulation, virtualized training, and assisted carrier landing technologies to prepare pilots for the demands of carrier operations. The JL-15, by contrast, is intended to support carrier-based pilot training. A dedicated carrier-capable trainer could offer China a more direct pathway for preparing pilots for operations aboard its increasingly sophisticated — and expanding — carrier fleet.
Taken together, the PLAN aircraft being lined up for Zhuhai this year illustrate the increasingly sophisticated and integrated nature of China’s carrier aviation ambitions . As well as the aircraft carriers and their embarked aircraft, these ambitions also require other surface and subsurface vessels to operate effectively.
Uncrewed systems will form another important part of the display. The exhibition will include aerial drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles, and other autonomous platforms, reflecting the PLAN’s growing interest in the potential of uncrewed warfare. articles.title_orig: Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict
articles.title_zh: Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict
articles.content_orig:
by Adriaan Alsema | Nov 23, 2026
A couple and their 18-year-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.
The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.
As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured.
The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.
An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.
Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.
The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.
In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.
De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.
According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.
The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.
All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

articles.title_orig: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.title_zh: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.content_orig:
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Political Leaders Denounce ‘Jewish Terrorism’ After West Bank Attacks
articles.title_zh: Israeli Political Leaders Denounce ‘Jewish Terrorism’ After West Bank Attacks
articles.content_orig:
Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank, burning cars and damaging property.
The attacks early on Sunday included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of homes in Ramallah and el-Bireh provinces, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The incidents were reported in Kafr Malik village, Deir Abu Mash’al village, and Deir al-Sudan village.
“Residents were awakened around two in the morning by sounds of fire and explosions. They realised the settlers had set fire to cars,” reported Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh from Kafr Malik.
Israeli settler violence has surged across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. At least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks there since Israel launched its war in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.
The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said there was a significant increase in the number of attacks throughout the Palestinian territory last month.
According to the Palestinian Authority body, there were 3,133 attacks in October, with Israeli forces responsible for 1,764 of them and Israeli settlers 1,369.
The commission said the total number of attacks increased by 53 percent compared with September when 2,051 attacks were recorded. Settler attacks alone rose from 647 in September to 1,369 in October – a 112 percent increase.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, who has been tasked with forming a new government after Israel’s general election last month, criticised the latest attacks on Sunday.
He wrote on social media that the attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is”.
“Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security of the state of Israel and its foreign relations,” he posted on X.
“The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy,” he added, referring to far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Ben-Gvir rejected the allegations and said Eisenkot was rushing to conclusions. He wrote on social media that Eisenkot’s stance represents a “down payment” to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi in preparation for forming a government with the support of Arab parties.
Settlers are often “escorted by Israeli squads and they do nothing to stop the attackers,” Shai Parnes of the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem told Al Jazeera.
The Israeli military said it was sending police officers and investigators from the Criminal Identification Unit to the attacked areas “to collect evidence as part of the ongoing investigation”, the military wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.title_zh: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.content_orig:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says .
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".
In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".
Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".
Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".
It said the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.content_orig:
No, it's not actually Black Friday itself for a few more days. But the annual sales event is now a week-long affair, and we traditionally start seeing some top deals from now.
It's confusing, we'll admit, but it does mean there is even more time to find some top deals.
And there's been some genuinely great savings in the worlds of hi-fi and home cinema already. Whether you're after a pair of budget Bluetooth headphones or a premium OLED TV, there's plenty of discounts to choose from.
And if you're not sure what to choose, that's where we come in. Our team of expert reviewers have tried and tested hundreds of hi-fi and home cinema products to find the very best.
Every deal below, unless flagged, features a product that has been reviewed and recommended by our testers, and is at a genuinely excellent price. We only recommend products that have four stars or more, and the best of the best will also have won a prestigious What Hi-Fi? Award.
We'll be here all week sharing deals and advice. And we're starting strong this Monday – take a look for yourself...
I’ve covered more Prime Days, Black Fridays and general AV sale events than I care to count. This, plus my experience as What Hi-Fi?’s editor-in-chief and a regular reviewer, gives me an expert knowledge of the market as a whole, which is why I’ll occasionally be chipping in here, offering my two cents on the top savings to jump at, and ones to avoid.
As the Deals Writer for What Hi-Fi?, I spend my days covering deals on all the latest TVs, soundbars, projectors, amps, speakers, headphones and more. I’ve spent years taking part in Black Friday both as a writer and a consumer, and know how important it is to cut through the noise to recommend the best value products. This week I’ll be constantly searching for new lowest prices and for ways to help our readers save money, but also making sure we’re highlighting products that are genuinely worth your money and have earned a recommendation from our rigorous review process.
I’m What Hi-Fi?’s TV & AV Editor, and I’ve been testing TVs and home cinema kit for almost 20 years. I love high-end gear, of course, but I also firmly believe that great picture and sound quality should be available to all. The good news is that you really don’t have to spend a fortune to get a home cinema experience to be proud of – especially if you shop around. I’m always on the hunt for big discounts, and Black Friday often unearths some great deals, but not all offers are as great as they might at first seem. Over the next few days, I will be flagging the real deals and warning you off the fake ones.
I run our hi-fi and audio section, and have spent over 14 years at What Hi-Fi? reviewing everything from premium turntables and stereo amplifiers to affordable DACs and speakers. Armed with plenty of advice, experience, and a desire to ensure everyone gets the ideal product for their needs and system, I will be able to tell you whether a Black Friday hi-fi deal is worth the plunge or not – and recommend better alternatives for better value.
The Apple AirPods Pro 3 may not be the tech giant's latest earbuds (that honour goes to the Apple AirPods 5 ), but they're still our favourites.
They're the ultimate in-ear Apple headphone experience, with the Pro 3 boasting better bass than their predecessors and active noise cancellation (ANC) that's twice as effective. There's also eight hours of battery life (24 hours including the case) and a fancy built-in heart rate sensor.
If you want all the snappy user-friendliness of Apple, our audio experts found the AirPods Pro 3 are the best all-around choice – and they're now at a new lowest price.
The Apple AirPods Pro 3 sound great, offer excellent ANC, deliver high comfort levels, and offer intuitive features unlike anyone else in the business. If you're after AirPods and can stretch to this price, then this is the model to buy
Want a good OLED TV but short on space?
We've got you covered. The LG C6 42-inch won not one, not two, but four What Hi-Fi? Awards, including Best 40- 43-inch TV.
This was thanks to its crisp, three-dimensional and contrast-rich picture and excellent motion handling, which made watching movies such as Blade Runner 2049 a highly cinematic experience despite the comparatively small screen size.
The C6 also won the Award for Best Gaming TV, so it is an ideal choice for GTA VI thanks to its stellar gaming specs that include VRR, ALLM, four high-speed HDMI 2.1 sockets and a wide array of cloud gaming apps.
Now available at a new lowest price – use the code SAVE50EXTRA to save £50 at checkout.
The LG C6 42-inch offers a crisp, three-dimensional and contrast-rich picture, along with excellent motion handling and gaming features. If you're short on space, this is our top choice for serious home cinema and gaming fans.
New to vinyl? Or getting back into it after several years off?
If you've got the budget to skip the cheapest entry-level models, then the Sony PS-LX5BT comes highly recommended by our audio experts.
The Bluetooth turntable is ideal for beginners, thanks to a built-in phono stage, fully automatic operation and great sonic performance for the price. It's simple to set up and use – simply press the 'start' and 'stop' buttons and the tonearm will move automatically.
If it's out of your budget, then the step-down model, the Sony PS-LX3BT , is also recommended and is currently around £80 cheaper. The LX5BT offers a more open, spacious and detailed sound, however, and is now available at a new low price.
With fully automatic operation, Bluetooth connectivity and an easy setup, the Sony PS-LX5BT is a great budget choice no matter your turntable knowledge. Together with a clear, cohesive and natural sound, the PS-LX5BT can do it all.
Price check: £282 at Sevenoaks
The JBL Live Pro 2 TWS tick a lot of boxes for not a lot of money, with one of the boxes including a rather stacked feature set.
ANC, IPX5 water resistance, a comfortable design and a thorough control app are all included, which made the bargain buds great value even at full price.
However, it's the lively and entertaining sound that really won us over, with expertly judged bass weight and superb detail levels.
And at £70, they're at a new lowest price with a whopping 46 per cent off!
The immensely likeable Live Pro 2 TWS offer plenty of bang for your buck, especially if you need lots of features without forking out a fortune.
Last week we highlighted a great deal on the Denon D-M41DAB , our favourite micro system and the benchmark for entry-level hi-fi.
Well, we're pleased to report that the deal is still live. The Award-winning micro system is still available, complete with speakers, for £299 at Amazon, which is a nice £100 saving.
The D-M41DAB is a convenient and affordable way to get into the world of hi-fi, with DAB, CD playback, Bluetooth streaming, and a remote control all included.
But most importantly, it sounds great, with superb sound quality that has won over the hearts of many What Hi-Fi? staff members over the years.
Combining a host of connectivity options with excellent sound quality, the Denon D-M41DAB budget micro hi-fi system is perfect for those with limited listening space who want to use various audio sources without sacrificing sound quality.
Looking for noise-cancelling headphones on a budget?
Then the Sony WH-CH730N are our over-ear recommendation.
Not only do they offer ANC (active noise cancellation) at this budget price, but there's also a bountiful feature set, outstanding battery life and a clear, detailed presentation included also.
The Award-winning headphones were only released in October, and just got their first discount when they dropped to £84 at Amazon last week. But we've just spotted the pair even cheaper – £79 at EE .

articles.title_zh: Phone Maker Nothing to Launch Earbuds and Case With AI Recording
articles.content_orig:
The new AI device from Nothing can record and transcribe audio with AI from the earbuds or via microphones on their charging case.﻿
The new AI device from Nothing can record and transcribe audio with AI from the earbuds or via microphones on their charging case.﻿
Nothing’s new AI device is the Ear Note, a set of earbuds and their microphone-equipped charging case that can record and transcribe conversations, with a connected app to manage the recordings, transcriptions and AI-generated summaries, similar to Apple’s new Watch feature and devices like Amazon’s Bee wearable . Nothing CEO Carl Pei demonstrated the new device to Bloomberg , but said the company hasn’t yet settled on a price ahead of a planned launch on December 8th.
The report also says Nothing’s rumored plans for an AI smartwatch and smart glasses are delayed, while it will be “pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.” In a post on X , Pei said this is “the first of many products building a hardware context layer for AI. Rather than ask you to carry a new product, we took something you already wear and trust and made it intelligent.”
According to Bloomberg, the earbuds will “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations.” Users will also be able to record themselves with a “Talk” button on the case, like Nothing previously included on the Ear 3 , which also has recording capabilities. Earlier this year, Nothing introduced an Audio Snapshot recording feature in the Ear 3A. Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max can also record directly to the earbuds’ case and generate AI transcripts and summaries in an app.

Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile
Now Bar live notifications
Samsung is moving its Now Bar live notifications closer to Apple's Dynamic Island, with changes to both their position and the way you switch between ongoing activities. We've tested the new layout in early Galaxy S27 series software.
Samsung is working on a new look for the Now Bar's live notifications, and the resemblance to Apple's Dynamic Island is hard to miss. We've exclusively discovered the changes in early Galaxy S27 series software, offering a glimpse of how Samsung could present ongoing activities in a future update.
On current versions of One UI, the live notification pill sits beside the clock on the left. Samsung's new layout moves it to the top center, in the area around the front camera.
The timer countdown, Torch indicator, and expandable activity controls you see here are familiar features already in One UI. The new layout displays those existing updates from this central position.
Centered torch Now Bar pill
Centered timer Now Bar pill
Samsung is also changing how you switch between compact live notification pills. Currently, you swipe up and down to move between ongoing activities. In the version we tested, you swipe left and right instead, without first expanding the pill.
That sideways switching gesture, combined with the placement around the selfie camera, gives Samsung's existing live notifications a more Dynamic Island-like feel.
Now Bar settings also include a Moment effects page, with Sports as the only listed download. It offers celebrations for your favorite teams' scores and wins in selected sports supported by Google Sports.
Samsung has already introduced sports animations in the One UI 9.5 beta . The broader Moment effects name could leave room for other types of effects later, but additional categories haven't been confirmed.
All of these changes are still under development and could be revised before Samsung brings them to Galaxy devices. They will likely debut with the Galaxy S27 series before reaching existing devices through the One UI 9.5 update .
First Samsung device: SGH-D500

In addition to phones and mobile devices, his interests include gaming on both PC and console, PC hardware, and spending countless hours on YouTube watching videos on tech, movies, games, politics, and internet dramas.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.title_zh: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday lauded an "exemplary" military operation that sank one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port, after Kyiv's forces struck their target with several domestically made naval drones.
The incident followed a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday and occurred less than a week after damage was inflicted on Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge.
In a social media post , Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces deployed seven sea drones to attack the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, at Benghazi's port in the early hours of Sunday morning. Ukraine's president posted dramatic video footage showing Ukraine's naval drones triggering a massive explosion on the Russian ship.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters," he added.
Satellite imagery taken on Sunday showed the Merkury mostly underwater, having capsized
The Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, was hit by Ukrainian forces. A Ka-27 military helicopter on the Merkury was also destroyed.
Asked about reports of attacks on Russian ships off the coast of Libya, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said information on this would be provided via the Defense Ministry.
The Security Service of Ukraine, the SBU, said Monday that the attacks "once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea," according to a Google translation.
"Such unique special operations destroy the enemy's logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for aggression even at a strategic distance from Ukraine," the SBU said via Telegram.
The United Nations Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, expressed "serious concern" over the drone attacks in a statement saying the country "cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts."
"UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added.
The incident is not the first time Libya has seen attacks linked to the Russia-Ukraine war near its territory.
In March, Moscow's Transport Ministry accused Ukraine of striking the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas tanker, as part of a suspected sea drone attack in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta.

articles.title_orig: Moscow accuses Estonia of hostile actions on 'verge of triggering open war'
articles.title_zh: Moscow accuses Estonia of hostile actions on 'verge of triggering open war'
articles.content_orig:
Russia has accused Estonia of carrying out numerous “hostile actions” and threatened “open war” against the neighbouring Baltic state.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday accused Tallinn of a ⁠⁠range of hostile actions, asserting that the NATO and European Union member state is “on ⁠⁠the verge of triggering open war”.
The outburst comes after Estonia announced the planned closure of its border with Russia, and a Ukrainian attack on a Russian ship in the Baltic Sea.
The ministry set out its accusations in a statement after ⁠⁠summoning Estonia’s charge d’affaires in Moscow, Marek Uhtegi, to issue a formal protest over Tallinn’s decision to close the border.
“The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering open war with Russia,” it said, adding that Estonia is displaying “Russophobic” tendencies.
Among a list of additional accusations, the ministry said Estonia had “tacitly allow[ed] its airspace to be used by Ukrainian drones for attacks on northwestern Russia”. Tallinn was swift to deny the claim.
It also accused Estonia of trying to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, banning the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain, seeking a ban on the Russian language and threatening to close the Russian Orthodox Church.
“The Russian side reserves the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens,” the ministry said.
Estonia is host to a sizeable ethnic Russian population, which Moscow has often claimed is subject to discrimination.
Russia’s incursions into eastern Ukraine in 2014 were based on claims of suppression of Russian speakers’ rights in the region.
Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close border crossings with Russia from December 1 for at least six months, having accused the Kremlin’s security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company.
This marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn – Kyiv’s ally – sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Russia has denied any involvement in the attack. Closing the border, the ministry said, “will inevitably backfire – not only on Tallinn itself but also on its allies within the EU and NATO”.
In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia did not respond to all of the allegations but denied that it allows its territory to be used for Ukrainian military operations.
“While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” it said.
“Other countries in our region have also made this position clear,” it added.
Russia has long accused Estonia and other NATO states in the Baltic region of allowing Ukrainian drones to use their airspace. Ukrainian drones have frequently entered NATO airspace, but Kyiv says this is a result of Russian signal jamming.
NATO countries have repeatedly denied intentionally allowing drones to use their airspace, and blamed Russia for the incursions.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking in Berlin, said the alliance was monitoring the situation in Estonia, along with an incursion last week by Russian missiles into Poland, adding that NATO had options available to respond.
“We see situations in Poland and Estonia, etc ,” Rutte said. “When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.”

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.
Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider said: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile."
Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.
Speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider said: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions."
Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.
"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.
"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures."
German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which said that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.
The reports said Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.
Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty , of which Moscow is a signatory.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said not allowing Ukraine into NATO in 2008 was a mistake.
At the 2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania , German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.
US President George W. Bush said he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.
But both Germany and France said that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance , but offered no timetable.
At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.
To which Merz said, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented."
Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.
Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.
"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said.
Merz said Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.
German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.
The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.
The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location."
"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.
A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics, AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.
The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.
Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.
The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.
Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.
They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.
More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.
Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark .
As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."
Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.
Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.
The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. T he second state co-chair still needs to be decided.
Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria .
The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU) , sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder . The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.
"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

A tech snafu at one of the world’s busiest airports on Sunday is delaying thousands of Delta Airlines flights headed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
An issue with Delta Airlines’ weight and balance system at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is responsible for the delay at one of the busiest airports in the country, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement posted on social media.
More than 3,550 flights traveling within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed as of Sunday afternoon, according to Flight Aware .
The governmental agency urged travelers to check in with the airline for the latest information on their flights, and said that steps have already been taken to fix the issue.
“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system,” the FAA statement said. “These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems.”
Delta said it is working limit congestion at its Atlanta hub.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” said Delta spokesperson Natalie Duggan. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."
The issue on Sunday comes after a communications failure grounded all flights nationwide earlier this month, leading New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to call for the removal of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Other recent technological malfunctions have impacted other industries, including online banking systems and Microsoft Outlook.
Delta Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Gothamist.

articles.title_orig: AI rally set to add $2 trillion to Nasdaq-100 as Huang returns to Nvidia helm
articles.title_zh: AI rally set to add $2 trillion to Nasdaq-100 as Huang returns to Nvidia helm
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent last week dumping anything tied to AI. It's spending Monday buying it back.
The Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ), the fund that tracks the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ), opened almost 8% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 1999. Its closest rivals for largest jumps came in 2000 and 2001 as the dot-com bubble was bursting and big rallies had a habit of fizzling.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened 5% higher. Among Mondays since 1993, only Oct. 13, 2008, in the depths of the financial crisis, started with a bigger jump.
The rally is holding. By midday, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is up more than 4% and on track for its best day since April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 is up more than 6%, and the CBOE Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) is down about 8 points.
The surge comes as Nvidia ( NVDA ) brought back Jensen Huang as CEO and after the S&P 500 slid into a correction last week.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) opened 15% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 2001 and well past its previous record of about 9% in October 2002.
Nvidia opened up 33% on Huang's return and is on track for one of the best days in the company's history, which tops out at a 42% gain in March 2000. Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ) opened roughly 12% to 21% higher.
Read more: Buy Nvidia stock or wait? A guide to making the call on any stock.
Not everyone thinks the panic has run its course. Options sentiment "screams" the worst levels since the pandemic and Liberation Day, Roundhill Investments chief investment strategist Drew Pettit told Yahoo Finance, "but it's not a washout."
History sides with the bulls, eventually. In the 20 times since 1993 that SPY opened Monday 2% or more higher, it was higher a year later in 17 of those, with a median gain of about 25%, roughly double that of a typical year, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello found a similar pattern . Last week's nearly 9% drop was the S&P 500's 12th-worst week since 1950, he noted, and after the worst weeks, stocks averaged a 26% gain over the next year, compared with 11% otherwise.
Evercore ISI's Julian Emanuel is in that camp too, writing over the weekend, "Bull Market intact as double-digit EPS gains likely ahead."
In half of those 20 cases, SPY slipped back below the prior Friday's low within three months, most often within two weeks. Think of it as the morning after a big night out. The headache usually comes back before it goes away.
Even so, eight of those 10 were higher a year later. The two closest matches to this setup, October 2008 and May 2010, each paired a brutal week with a big Monday open, sank further over the next three months and were about 15% higher a year later.
That puts Friday's low, about 6,883 on the S&P 500, in focus. And the Fed isn't riding to the rescue , with Wall Street still pricing a December rate hike and every correction that hits with inflation speeding up this fast turning into a bear market .
BTIG's strategists aren't calling a bottom yet. "We don't think this is the final low, but we are looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again," they wrote over the weekend.
As of midday Monday, the S&P 500 is already knocking on the bottom of that range.

Update [ Mon 23rd Nov 2026, 2:50pm ]: Well, the patch notes are out! Rockstar Games mentions seven official fixes for the update, and none of them are specifically to do with the Xbox Series S or other things like how bright the game is.
Nevertheless, there's always a chance they've made some extra tweaks under the hood.
Here are the official seven fixes in GTA 6's first post-launch update (November 23):
Original Story: GTA 6 only officially launched late last week, but Rockstar Games has already pushed out a new update (01.002.002) for the game across Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with PS5), rolling out as of a few hours ago.
You're looking at a download size of around 1.6GB for update 1.0.2 on Xbox Series X and S.
In terms of what's included, Rockstar has yet to issue any official patch notes, and we'll have to wait and see whether anything is distributed. We'll obviously update this article with the patch notes if they're made available to us.
Players are trying to make their own discoveries in the meantime, with suggestions that the game may run smoother on Xbox Series S now, that saving your game returns you to the exact same spot instead of your safehouse (although this seemed to be happening for us already), and that the first-person glitch is still working as things stand.
All of these could be akin to placebo effects though, so take them with a pinch of salt:
As you can see from one of the impressions above, there's a suggestion that the game seems brighter now, which perhaps could have something to do with the borked HDR calibration tool that we discussed the other day .
That said, who knows whether these are areas that have actually been targeted for the update, or whether they're just happy coincidences that some players are experiencing. In any case, we'll keep an eye out for any official confirmations.

articles.title_orig: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.title_zh: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.content_orig:
Every year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say.
Net investment income tax , or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act .
Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets , the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.
As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.
Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021.
As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.
NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado , CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida.
"The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council .
For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income , or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return .
MAGI limits by filing status
Married filing jointly: $250,000
Married filing separately: $125,000
Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000
Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000
NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale , for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.
The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.
The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:
For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.
Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.
As year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say.
If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.
While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026.
You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals.
Amid recent stock market volatility , investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting , which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said.
If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.
However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the " wash sale rule ," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas has extended his contract with the ⁠chip designer to lead the company through 2033, confirming his ​leadership role ​at the ​firm amid speculation that Nvidia could tap him for the top job after Jensen Huang's resignation.
Nvidia's board ⁠had ‌approached Haas in its search ⁠for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times reported earlier this month, following Huang's exit amid revelations of extramarital affairs ‌including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Analysts had also pointed to Haas ​as a solid candidate for the CEO role at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company, rising to ⁠vice president and general manager of its computing products ‌business, before joining Arm in ‌2013.
Haas became the British chipmaker's chief executive in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets ⁠through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year.
Arm licenses ⁠processor designs used across smartphones, ⁠PCs, servers and connected devices.
"I've never been more confident about Arm's future... I'm wholly ​committed to realizing ‌Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday.
Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of ​SoftBank Group , effective December 1, Arm ‌Holdings said on Monday.

articles.title_orig: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.title_zh: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 09:37 EST, 23 November 2026
As stock market debuts go, it certainly lived up to the hype.
Anthropic shares soared by nearly 40 per cent in the first minutes of trading in New York last Thursday – giving it a value of more than $2trillion.
Its seven founders, all in their 30s and 40s, including Brighton-born Jack Clark, were sitting on fortunes of $26billion each. Thousands more staff were millionaires many times over.
So, was the blockbuster float the tonic Wall Street needed after weeks of market turmoil?
The AI developer, best known for its Claude chatbot, surrendered early gains though still ended its first session of trading up 17 per cent. On Friday, it crashed back to the $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent.
More worrying still, trading screens were a sea of red from east to west, with the MSCI All Country World Index, a key benchmark of global stocks, suffering its longest losing streak for three years.
Once again, it was technology stocks that bore the brunt of the sell-off, with New York’s blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index now down by more than 18 per cent from its peak a little over a month ago.
Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Friday morning, after AI developer Anthropic debuted on the stock market. It crashed back to its $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent
Among the AI pioneers that had led the charge earlier in the year – the hyperscalers, the neoclouds, the data centre developers – it was carnage.
Since reaching record highs in recent months, CoreWeave, SanDisk and Nebius are down some 70 per cent, while Intel and Oracle have fallen around 60 per cent. The list goes on.
Nvidia – the posterchild of the AI revolution that was left reeling from the sudden departure of rockstar boss Jensen Huang over a string of affairs before his dramatic reinstatement on Monday – was down more than 40 per cent in a rout that wiped around $2.5trillion off the value of what was once the world’s biggest company.
Nvidia shares bounced back after on Monday as investors welcomed his return. Tech stocks also rallied - but the outlook remains deeply uncertain.
‘We’re already in a stealth bear market,’ notes one Mayfair-based hedge fund manager. This refers to a market in which a specific sector falls 20 per cent or more from its peak.
The big question before Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) was whether it would be enough to save the AI trade and restore faith in the stuttering stock market.
The answer was a resounding no – and many of the world’s top investors are fearful of what comes next.
They are not alone. Wall Street’s so-called ‘fear index’ – the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) – is at its highest level since March, when markets were shuddering at the sound of Donald Trump’s war on Iran.
‘A week from hell,’ is how Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, referred to last week.
‘It’s gritty out there,’ says a respected City fund manager who looks after hundreds of millions of pounds of savings. ‘People have ploughed headlong into the US without thinking about valuation. There’s a period of adjustment ahead. We’ll have to see how long and how bad it is.’
For two of America’s most prominent investors – Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and Ken Griffin, of rival Citadel – we are in the midst of a bubble that is one day bound to burst.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Dalio.
Berkshire Hathaway, which was the home of the ‘Oracle of Omaha’ – Warren Buffett – for six decades until he stood down as chairman in September, now holds a staggering $377.4billion in cash.
While this does not necessarily mean he believes a crash is coming, at the very least it shows he does not think many stocks offer good value at their current prices.
Owen Lamont, a fund manager at Acadian Asset Management in Boston and a former University of Chicago finance professor, notes that as recently as January he penned an article titled ‘We are not in an AI bubble’.
‘Today, I would no longer write those words,’ he says. ‘I think there is a 70 per cent chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the US stock market. The smart money is selling.’
Closer to home, the head of market strategy at one of the City’s leading investment banks is more convinced than ever that the bubble is about to burst, so much so he has sold his own private share holdings.
‘We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish,’ says Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum. ‘We think the AI bubble is about to burst. Market dynamics have turned decisively bearish.’
The trigger for his own decision to sell – and move money into government bonds – was the S&P 500 moving below a key threshold known as the 200-day moving average.
‘I know I will be out of stocks when the AI bubble bursts,’ he says.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates
Gary Channon, a fund manager at Phoenix Asset Management in London, is similarly pessimistic. He says: 'The current bubble has almost run its course. It has been a great ride, but the building is on fire, save yourselves.’
Whether or not a crash is coming, one thing is for sure, according to one of London’s leading fund managers: ‘A lot of people have already been very badly burned.’
He explains: ‘In the first half of this year, there has been a lot of FOMO in the market, or fear of missing out, with a lot of unsophisticated investors going into AI. The last few months have been very painful for them.’
A crash would spell misery for millions of British savers with money tied up in shares through their pensions, stocks and shares Isas and other investments.
The London stock market – with its banks, oil majors and pharmaceutical groups, but very few tech stocks – has fared better than its US counterparts in the recent turmoil.
On November 16, the FTSE 100 came within a whisker of a new record close. The mood has darkened since then however, as storm clouds drift over the Atlantic, and London’s premier shares index racked up losses of 5 per cent in just five days last week.
Panmure’s Klement believes ‘UK stocks are the best hiding place’ from the turmoil – identifying companies from GSK and AstraZeneca to Greggs and Wetherspoon.
‘After all, if the market crashes, what else can you do but go to a pub?’ he notes ruefully, adding that, in fact, ‘the best positions to take are cash and the foetal position’.
Such is the might of US tech, the bursting of the AI bubble could drag global markets down with it.
And it is not just Wall Street that is suffering.
Asian shares clocked up their worst week since 2020. Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 5 per cent on Friday alone, while Taiwanese shares were down 17 per cent in their biggest weekly decline since 1990.
There has been no shortage of warnings from global regulators, with almost every financial enforcer on Earth sounding the alarm, from the International Monetary Fund to the world’s central bank chiefs.
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned the vast sums borrowed by the AI industry to fund the revolution are now a risk to financial stability.
And Boris Vujcic, vice president at the European Central Bank, has spoken of an ‘abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses’ in stock markets – which sounds a lot like a crash – if investor sentiment about AI suddenly sours.
This could hardly come at a worse time.
The global economy is reeling from an energy price shock – stemming first from Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and then Trump’s war in Iran – that is squeezing households and businesses alike.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Faces Fresh Questions Over China Chip Smuggling Probe
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a May 2026 ceremony in China. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title_orig: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.title_zh: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”
